utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... continue. Please be aware that the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your evidence to tell the truth continues to apply to your evidence today. And cross-examination will now continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, before we move on to another topic that we did not discuss yesterday I would like to briefly touch upon some things that we did discuss yesterday so that we can be clear in our minds before we proceed today. First of all, the Judge has just reminded you of the solemn declaration that you took yesterday that is still in effect. Do you understand the solemn declaration that you gave yesterday to tell the truth in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And yesterday when you said you had not seen either of the prosecutors prior to giving your testimony and that you did not meet with them to discuss your statement, that was not the entire truth; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: It's not true that I met them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, did you not hear yesterday when the Prosecutor's Office in fact confirmed that they did meet with you prior to your testimony? Are they not telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I did not meet them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it still your testimony that you did not speak with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I only gave a statement and I signed my statement at the place where I gave the statement, and it was a correct statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: This was in 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, in fact, I submit that you met with the prosecutors, as they stipulated yesterday, that you met with them on August the 19th, 2006, and I submit that, when you met with them, you told them that this Rambo that you described, that his uniform was not the regular police uniform. Isn't that the truth, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: He had the uniform that I described yesterday, with a cap, with a bill. He had an emblem on his cap. On the right arm there was this inscription, policija. He had a badge and the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, during questions put forth to you by the Trial Chamber, by Judge Bonomy, you said that the police did not have blue uniforms, and that was not the truth either, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: No. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, I submit that the employees of the Ministry of the Interior, the police, do have blue uniforms but due to your problem with differentiating colours you have a hard time seeing the difference between blue and green. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Well, I said what I knew and what I said I'm sure about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I can touch upon yet again the -- the April 3rd, 1999, incident, you had stated that although the police had not expelled you from your home, that another group had done that, you said you saw police on the street. Where were the police on the street? That is to say, how far away were they from your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: The police were 200 metres from my home, along the road there were regular policemen, up to the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you describe whether these persons you have described as regular police, whether they had any badges, insignia, or other emblems on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: They had the same, the normal badges. On the right arm there was the inscription "policija," and they had on their caps the emblem of Serbia. I said the same uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you -- yesterday you testified that the regular police of the Ministry of the Interior did not have insignia on their hats. Are you not --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, could we have a page and line reference, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Transcript page 76, line 10. And I will -- just so that the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I said the same thing yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At line 7 my question to you yesterday was, "You mentioned head-gear. During your time spent in Pristina, what time of head-gear did the normal police have?" Answer at line 9: "The normal police had caps of the same colour as their clothes but they didn't have insignia on the caps." So which is the truth, sir? Did the police, the employees of the Ministry of the Interior, did they have insignia or did they not have insignia on their caps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Well, I said the same yesterday. Maybe I forgot but on their caps they had the insignia of Serbia. On the arm -- they had "policija" written on their arms, and on their chest they had badges. They had belts as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to move on to another area. In the statement that is being proffered as evidence in these proceedings, the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, you state your belief that the man Rambo was one of the people that assaulted your wife. Now, what I want to ask you is, is your belief that Rambo was one of the attackers based upon your speculation due to prior incidents and encounters that you had with Rambo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Well, I did not encounter Rambo there. I just suspected that he had been there because, according to my wife's words, they had different uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does your wife know Rambo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: No. No, she doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it your belief that Rambo had a personal vendetta against you for some reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: That's what I thought, but how true that is, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And isn't it a fact that the person who described the uniforms of the attackers, the person who assaulted your wife, was in fact your neighbour rather than your wife?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I did not understand the question. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is the person who described the uniforms of the attackers who assaulted your wife, was that person your neighbour rather than your wife, that told you about the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Not the neighbour but my wife told me about the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to direct your attention to paragraph 29 of your statement. Do you still have that statement in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Before I ask my question I'm going to caution you on one thing. You are testifying here under protective measures so I will not use the name of your neighbour so as to preserve your confidentiality. I would also remind you, please, to not use her name, which is listed in this paragraph. And my question to you, sir, would be, if you have time to read this paragraph: Isn't it true that this paragraph of your statement describes that your neighbour actually told you -- is the one that told you that your wife had been assaulted by three police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: My wife told me about the case. It is true that the neighbour called me, phoned me, and told me to come urgently. But my wife told me about the uniforms and the persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, isn't it a fact that yesterday in your testimony, at page 67, lines 9 through 12, when testifying about this incident and your knowledge of it, you said, and I quote, "At that moment, she said" -- strike that. Let me start from line 8 so it's clear. My question to you yesterday -- or, excuse me, I believe it was the Prosecutor's question to you yesterday: "Did your wife describe the men to you who raped her?" Answer, at line 9: "At that moment, she said there were three paramilitaries with -- wearing masks, black masks, camouflage uniforms, and at that moment, in fact, she wasn't sure what the uniform -- what the uniforms were like, just that they had masks on their faces." Does that comport to the testimony that you just gave us today and if not, which is the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I told you yesterday and I will repeat it today, when I went home, I saw my wife tearing at her face. I told -- I asked her, What has happened? And she told me that she was raped by three policemen, paramilitaries. I don't know how to describe them. And the truth is what she told me. That's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, you don't know how to describe them because you did not see the uniforms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Of course I did not see the uniforms because I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And your wife would be the best person to describe those uniforms; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Of course. She is the one because it happened to her not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could leave that incident and that date by the side, I would like to just ask a couple more questions relating to April the 3rd and the events that you testified to following your expulsion from your home. Now, is it -- am I correct that you set forth in your statement that there were -- that there was -- that there were Serb civilians expressing animosity towards yourself and others that were -- that were leaving Pristina on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, when we left our home, this didn't happen, but on the way, en route, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would it be safe to say that as a result of the NATO bombings, the attitude of civilians of Serb and other ethnicities in Pristina became rather elevated or heightened, emotionally heightened, as a result of the bombings? Would that be a fair appraisal of the environment in Pristina as a result of the NATO bombings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: It's not true that the NATO bombing caused that, because if that were true, all the Serbs and Albanians would have left but the fact is that only the Albanians were expelled. The Serbs did not leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I don't think you understood my question. Let me rephrase it. Did you notice Serb civilians becoming agitated in their interactions towards Albanian, ethnic Albanian civilians, after the commencement of NATO bombings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, on the day in question, April 3rd, 1999, at that point in time, did you witness civilians who were antagonistic towards yourself and others who were leaving Pristina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And did you see any organs of the state, any forces attempting to keep these angry Serb civilians from getting close to you and the other persons who were leaving Pristina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I'm done. If I could just have a brief moment to look over my notes to confirm that, and then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I thank you for your time. I'm finished with my questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions either, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As opposed to the rest, I don't have any questions either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I have one, hopefully one question for the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Witness, could you look at me, please? Do you recall -- and I take off the headphones so you can see me clearly. Do you recall that you met with me and my colleague sitting here to my right on last Saturday and we went over your statement with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes. Now that I can see your faces, yes. But I didn't know your names.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: But you recall now that you indeed meet -- met with us on the 19th of August? Do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That completes my questioning, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if you can help me try to understand something about your evidence. You were asked yesterday and also first thing today about meeting two of the prosecutors in the case last Saturday, and both yesterday and today you denied that such had -- such a meeting had taken place. And we now learn that there was such a meeting. Why did you deny that there was a meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I didn't realise who they were, who the people in the Prosecution were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That won't do. The question wasn't about identified people. The question was whether you had met people from the Prosecution. Now, why did you deny that there was ever such a meeting last Saturday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I can only say that I didn't realise that they were from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again I repeat, that won't do. You have given an undertaking to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Whether or not you're familiar with that in your own experience doesn't matter. The words are very simple: To tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Now, I want you to give me a reason that I understand for denying that such a meeting took place. Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I did not know that they were from the Prosecution. I don't know what else to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who did you think they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I wasn't really aware of who they were because people accompany us, talk to us, bring us into offices for talks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think I'm bound to make it clear to you, I just do not accept -- I, for one, do not accept that you did not know who you were talking to. We are assisted here by responsible people whose duty it is to make it clear to you who they are before they speak to you. Now, I'll give you one final opportunity to tell me why it is that you denied that that meeting took place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-63
utterances.text: I did not deny it for any particular -- for any reason. I just didn't know who they were. I've never been here before. I don't know who the prosecutors are, who the Judges are, I don't know who is who. And I don't know what "Prosecutor" means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, witness, that completes your evidence to the Tribunal. We are grateful to you for coming to give evidence. It is our job, though, to ask any questions that we feel are necessary to clarify the position and that's why additional questions have been asked in this case. But that now completes your evidence and you're free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is Ms. Moeller to deal with the next witness or Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller is, Your Honour, but before she does, may I address what matter to you? It is my -- it is our standard practice to usually go out and speak to a witness after they've testified, and that was my intention, to do that now, but in light much your concerns and the questions addressed to him at the end, I don't know if you would rather I not speak with him for a while?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I have no problem with you following your normal practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So thank you, Mr. Hannis. Yes, the next witness, Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness is Witness K-62, and she's a live witness. Her testimony relates to paragraph 72(G), 77(A) and (C).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to keep you waiting there but I didn't want to speak over the noise of the blinds. Could you please take the solemn declaration by reading aloud the document which is now in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing -- I solemnly declare that I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. Now, I'd like to explain to you at the outset that we already have in front of us a written statement of evidence to be presented by you, and we are aware of the sensitive nature of the events that you will describe. And all of us have experience of people who have had to suffer similar tragedies in their lives and regrettably have had to come and tell others about it and we understand how difficult that exercise can be. So if at any stage you require respite from giving evidence, just tell me, but I can also say to you from experience that it sometimes helps to take a deep breath and do your best to carry on because one way or another we just have to do our best to get through it. So you're now to be asked a number of questions by the counsel representing parties in this case, the Prosecution and the Defence, and some of them may be questions which challenge what you've said in your statement. Don't be surprised by that. That's part of the system that we operate under. You wouldn't be here unless somebody was expected to be challenging something that you said in the statement. That's just part of the normal process. But what we require is the most honest account we can possibly get of the events and the most honest answers we can get to the questions that are asked. The first person to ask questions will be for the Prosecution, Ms. Moeller. Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could the usher take the identification sheet to the witness? This is Exhibit P2265 and it was tendered under seal yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at that sheet and see whether this is your name on there, correctly? And don't say your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I think the sheet has already been shown yesterday to Your Honours and to the Defence. It's in evidence so you can take it away. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: What is your ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: I'm Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could the usher take another sheet, please, to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: There is Exhibit P2266 and it was also tendered under seal yesterday, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at this sheet and confirm whether this is the name of your husband?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you live in 1998 and 1999, Madam?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: In Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how did you and your husband earn your living at this time in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: We worked. Firstly we worked together and then we were expelled from our jobs and then we opened a shop but it didn't go well so we closed it. And then we worked in the private market in a pizzeria, and then we opened a burek shop. And that's what we did until we were expelled from our home.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: When the NATO bombing started in March 1999, where were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: At home.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Why were you not at the shop helping your husband?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: I did go from time to time, but I was scared at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what were you scared of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: I was afraid of the paramilitaries and the police around. There were a lot of police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what were they doing? What made you afraid of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: I was afraid because I saw them in front of the shop I was working and they were beating up the children. There were children selling cigarettes and they would take their cigarettes without paying for them. They were beating people and taking their money away; they wouldn't pay for things. They were bothering people playing Bingo and taking their money.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how was the general situation in Pristina in March 1999? How many people were in the city approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: I can't tell you, but many people came from other places, came into town, and others left. There were too many people in the apartments. It was very difficult for us. We would open up our apartments, some were closed, some opened, people came in from the country-side, from all over the place. We didn't know what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Do you know why these people came into the town from the country-side, as you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: They were afraid. They were being thrown out of their homes, expelled from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how did you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: How I found out? I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: From whom did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: The people themselves, the people who lost their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: How was your life during these days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: It was all right up until then but then it became very difficult after April, after the 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Before the 1st of April, how did you get your food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: Sometimes we bought food from the neighbours. There were shops around. There was a burek shop there and we would get food and take it home and cook it at home. We took food from our own shop. We cooked when there was electricity but often the electricity was off and there was no telephone either, so we had to stock up food in advance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Around the time the NATO bombing started, and before 1st April, did you meet anyone in Pristina that you knew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: I lived in town. I met people, all sorts of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Baton Haxhiu?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He was a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did you know his father?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Where did you know him from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: I knew because he came and lived in a neighbouring apartment on the -- I think it was the third floor, with Baton.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when did you last speak to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: I can't remember when I last spoke to Baton but I did talk to the father. I met Baton's father in Brigoj e Dilit [phoen] neighbourhood, and he was so beaten up I couldn't even recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Did he say anything to you, why he was so beaten up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: They beat him up because they were looking for his son. They spread rumours that his son had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And he told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "He spread rumours himself that his son had been killed."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Let us now move to the 1st of April 1999. Where were you on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: I was at home on the 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And where were your husband on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: He was in the shop.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: How was the situation in your neighbourhood that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: I don't know how to explain it. It's difficult for me. I thought that it was my husband knocking at the door. It was about 12.30 in the afternoon, but it was not him. It was three other people. I thought maybe they came to loot, and I would give them everything. I just didn't want them to touch me. One of them was -- the other -- the two of them were searching the rooms while one of them did whatever he wanted with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can I stop here, Witness? Could we go into private session here, Your Honours? Please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. In view of the nature of the evidence that you are seeking to elicit, we will go into private session. I just invite you to restrict the evidence as far as you possibly can within reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I will try my best.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: After the 1st of April, how long did you continue to stay in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: Two more nights.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And why did you leave then? That was on the 3rd of April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: The 3rd of April, we were expelled from our homes because we didn't want to leave our homes, but it was not possible to stay because otherwise, if we did not leave, they would kill us. These people came in masks and they told us to go to the railway station, all the roads and all the streets were full of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You just said, "they expelled us." Who were "they"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: It was the paramilitaries. That's how we called them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: How did they look?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: Their clothes were green and black, dark green and brown and black, camouflage. I will never forget them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You just said a minute ago the roads and all the streets were full of people. Who were these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: People from town.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Of which ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: Albanians. Everybody was trying to protect themselves. They were all lining up, going to the station, to the railway station, to take us to Bllaca. We did not know where we were going but that's where they took us, to Bllaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Did you see any Serbs being in that -- the group of people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: I didn't hear anybody speak in Serb. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So you said you were told to go to the railway station. What happened at the railway station, the Pristina railway station, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: I thought I would die. It was -- we were so close to each other, I could not breathe. People came to ask for money. We did not know how much money we had to pay. Everybody gave what they had. Such a crowd, such a crowd. Nobody knew who was the conductor of the train. They came and asked for money and we gave lots of money to them. I think we paid at least 3 times the fare, the normal fare.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you already told the Court that you were taken to Bllaca with this train. How many people do you think were at Bllaca with you? Can you give an estimate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you. The whole of Pristina was there, lying down, sick people, all there. Everybody was sick. The rain was falling. Every three seconds, I had to go. It was cold. The rain was falling on us and we just slept like that outside. We got colds there. The conditions were horrible. I can't tell you how horrible they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And where did you go from Bllaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: From Bllaca, we were taken to tents. I got separated from my husband. You can't imagine how difficult that was for me. Nobody knows that but me. We were taken by bus to some tents. I was taken to a certain tent. And two months after we got separated, the Red Cross helped us to get together. It was so difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Madam, how is your health today, after all that happened to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: My health, well, if somebody sees me today, after so many years, they wouldn't believe it's me. I have no desire to buy clothes and to maintain myself. My face has changed. My body has changed. I buy children-sized clothes now. I used to take care of myself a lot and I loved clothes and everything. Now I don't. I don't care. As I said, I buy children-sized clothes. I can't eat. I think my stomach has shrunk, and my teeth now are so bad because of all these medicines I take. My God, my God.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would conclude my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Moeller. Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We'll proceed in this order: Counsel for General Lukic, General Pavkovic, and thereafter, the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam my name is Dan Ivetic, and along with Branko Lukic and Ozren Ogrizovic, I represent Mr. Sreten Lukic. Now, I know it's difficult for you to testify about some of the things you have testified about today. I will try and make this process as smooth as possible so as to minimise any discomfort to you. But please understand that I have to ask questions to try and understand your testimony a bit better and to help in the process of finding out exactly what had happened in Pristina during the relevant time period. Now, first of all, I want to ask you if you recall giving a statement to investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor in 2003, in May of 2003.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, ma'am. Was that a yes? We have to have vocal answers otherwise we can't be certain.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And at that time, was the statement read back to you in Albanian so that you could understand it and confirm that everything contained therein was accurate, in terms of reflecting the truth of what you had told the investigator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: No. I will never forget the problems I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, ma'am. I apologise. Perhaps my question was compound and difficult to answer. The statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in May of 2003, was that statement read back to you in the Albanian language so that you could understand it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: You mean did they do it? I have forgotten, I don't know whether I read it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: I gave a -- the statement in 2003. Do you mean is that -- do you mean did I read that one again?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking, ma'am, if -- ma'am, if anyone at that time in 2003 read back that statement to you in the Albanian language so that you could understand it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: Yes. What I said was translated into English because I don't know English. What I said, my words, were translated but that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, ma'am, thank you. And then you in fact signed the English text of that statement in 2003; is that correct? After it had been translated to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's get to the point you want to make. We know that this is a very circuitous route that doesn't really take our understanding of matters any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying to establish that she did sign the statement and that the statement contains --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's not a jury you're in front of. I've told you this before, Mr. Ivetic. We can see that it's signed. We don't need these things spelled out to us as a foundation in the way that you might deal with them before a jury.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour. But for purposes of the record I believe we do need to have them into the record so as to have a complete record for purposes of these proceedings. I appreciate that the -- that the Trial Chamber is professional and versed in these matters but for the record and -- of these proceedings, I believe that we have to. But I will try to short-circuit some of that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, what would have helped would have been to have this statement as an exhibit. And it could have been shown to the witness and we could have expedited the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not have the statement in Albanian so I could not do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The signature was of an English copy, as I understand it; that's what the questions are about, signing an English copy. And it would have helped to have it, to see her signature, and she could have short-circuited this exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: True, but the -- I don't think the English statement would have helped refresh her recollection as to what was done with the statement and whether it was read back to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's when we get to the real issue. I'm talking about these procedural niceties that you seem to be so intent upon pursuing in each case, which I, yet again, suggest to you are unnecessary for our purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. I will try to short-circuit those for my examinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Madam, first of all, I would like to ask you a couple of questions from your -- relative to your husband. Now, during the time that you have known him, have you noticed any visual acuity problems?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: Could you start that again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure. During the time that you've known your husband, have you noticed any visual acuity problems? That is to say, any difficulties distinguishing between any colours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: Yes, many. When I send him to buy something, he doesn't understand the colours of the things. He can distinguish white and black but the other colours he gets mixed up. He's very confused in colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. That clarifies things greatly for me. Now, during the time period that you lived and worked in Pristina, and now I'm talking -- well, during the entire time period that you lived and worked in Pristina, when you saw policemen on the street, that is to say uniformed members of the Ministry of the Interior, what kind of uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: The normal uniforms had "police" written on them. They were normal uniforms. For instance, was either black or white, but the policemen always had a badge and we knew they were policemen because it said "policemen." They were normal municipal policemen, normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And ma'am, now I have to ask you, with respect to these -- what you've described as normal uniforms, what -- was there any pattern on them, with the colours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: Well, they had a badge and they were policemen. We knew they were policemen. They were the normal police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as part of the uniforms of the police, was there also any type of hat or head-gear and, if there was, could you describe it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: Of the policemen earlier, you mean? I can't really tell you whether they wore hats. I wasn't paying attention to things like that, about the policemen at the time. I didn't have any problems or any encounters with the police. I was never paying attention to what -- to whether they were wearing hats or not but I do know that they were all wearing the same uniforms and we could recognise them as policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And would it be accurate to state that these uniforms that the policemen wore on a daily basis were not green in colour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: They had -- the people who expelled us from our homes were not policemen. They had different uniforms. They had masks and had long boots and green uniforms and masks. They were not the same as the police. These people came into my house. I will never forget them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can understand that, ma'am. Now, if I can draw your attention and I know it's difficult but let's start with March 31st of 1999. I believe that you had an encounter with some people that came to your home on March 31st of 1999. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: People came to help me but I didn't want them to -- I was afraid. I didn't want too many people around me because they --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me try and assist you. I understand you've already discussed what happened to you on April the 1st of 1999, when the three men came to your apartment. I don't want to repeat that incident. I'm talking about the day before. Do you recall the day before that event, that some men came to your home, to your apartment, on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: Yes. They came because they wanted a place to spend the night. But it was in the basement but we didn't want them to. We didn't want them. They wanted to bring their whole families with them and there was no room.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I try to direct you: Specifically, do you remember an encounter with some men in uniforms that came to your home on the night before the instance where you were assaulted by three men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: They came to loot and to take things. They came to all the houses in the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And ma'am, these men that came in uniforms, did they have the same uniforms as the three men that came on April 1st and assaulted you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: Yes, the same, the same uniform; not policemen, the uniform was the same as the one I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you're very clear that these individuals were not policemen, were not from the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: No. I'm sure, a hundred per cent, that they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. Now, if you could please direct your attention now to the events of April the 3rd 1999, when you stated that men came and expelled you from your home. At that point in time, when you were expelled from your home, is it accurate to state that none of the men engaged in expelling you from your home and forcing you to the train station, none of them were wearing uniforms that you would describe as being police uniforms of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: No, they had the same uniform as the people who came into our house. They were not policemen. There weren't policemen. I mean the ones that expelled us from our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And ma'am, at that point in time, you were with your husband; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At all times, up until the point where you said you were separated from him, he was with you; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And during that period of time, is it accurate to state that there were no police present participating in any of the events between the time that you were expelled from your home and the time that you arrived at the train station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: No. I did not see a single policeman. I can't say that I did when I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I am finished with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we don't have questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk? And

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any re-examination, Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Madam, Judge Chowhan as a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I just want to ask you, that incident you described very explicitly before us, did you suffer from any medical -- any disease of your body, ever since then? Did you have any other disease you suffered from or -- because of consequences and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-62
utterances.text: Illness? Well, my emotional state is not right. That's the biggest illness I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Madam. That completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. We are going to adjourn now, if you just remain where you are, arrangements will be made to escort you from the courtroom in a moment. And the Chamber will now adjourn and will resume at 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The next witness, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm not sure the next witness has arrived yet because of how quickly things went this afternoon. I was told right before the break it was going to take 30 minutes for him to get here. I was advised just a minute ago that he -- he is on the way but I'm not sure if he's here yet. In the meantime, there was one matter I wanted to address with Your Honour concerning this municipality. We had an additional witness that we had proposed as a 92 bis(C) witness. This is Anthony Russo [phoen]. He's deceased. In the Court's prior ruling regarding the 92 bis evidence, I'll quote, the Court stated that, quote, "The written statement of Mr. Russo is directly relevant to crimes allegedly committed in Pristina in 1999. It is thus relevant crime base evidence. It is also cumulative and said to be corroborative of the evidence of proposed witnesses Nazlie Bala and Emin Kabashi, who may be cross-examined. The trial court thus considers it appropriate to admit the evidence albeit cross-examination is not possible." The court didn't go on to rule at that time, it indicated that if the evidence is ultimately admitted, the Trial Chamber will have very much in mind the absence of the opportunity to cross-examine him. Because now we've finished with our crime-base witnesses for Pristina I wanted to bring it to your attention at this time and tender it. It is Exhibit P2261. And I ask to you take it into consideration at this time in connection with those other Pristina witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Does any Defence counsel have anything to say on this? Very well. That will be admitted in terms of 92 bis(C).

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, our next witness will be Milazim Thaqi, T-h-a-c-i [sic]. His evidence pertains in particular to events in Izbica village, Skenderaj, or Srbica municipality, and relates in particular to paragraph 72(C) and 75(F) as well as schedule F to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he is a witness we are proceeding with under Rule 92 bis(D), Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. My name is Milazim Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, take your time to -- yeah, please adjust these so that they are comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a little tight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Thaqi, we have before us already a copy of a statement that you have made. We also have a written record of the evidence which you gave when you were here before. So we know a great deal already about what you have to say. And the purpose of this afternoon's hearing is to allow the counsel involved in the case to ask you some further questions. And the first counsel to ask questions of you will be for the Prosecution, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you tell us your name, please, your full name?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: My name is Milazim Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Thaqi, I understand that you were born in 1946, you have always lived in the village of Broja --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You have always lived --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And that you are a Kosovar Albanian Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as the judge indicated, we do have a transcript of your prior testimony in the Milosevic case, and your prior written statements, which are in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, we would tender those at this time, 22 -- P2247 being the transcript and P2246 being his 92 bis package.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, did you have a chance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you go on, Mr. Hannis, apart from his statement, is there anything else in that 92 bis package? I think there may be photographs, are there?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There is a photograph that was attached to his statement which has a separate exhibit number and which I will show him later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll deal with that. There are actually -- I've got copies of three photographs here and I have two statements; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe there are two statements. One shorter statement that deals with the aerial photograph of the area and there were three photographs of clothing with holes in them, which he relates to in his statement as the clothing he was wearing the day the shootings occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And these are still attached to a statement as part of this package, are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: They are included within that page range, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the two interviews were in November 1999 and October 2001?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, did you have a chance to go over your statements with me and Ms. Fikirini here yesterday, briefly, to see if there were any corrections?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if I may --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: It was fine. Everything was all right. Everything that I read was all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may direct your attention, I believe there were two -- two places where you indicated that there were -- there were things that needed to be corrected. On page 6 of the English, paragraph 4, you talk about when on April 7th you were reunited with your family, and in the English statement, it says that happened at Tushica, and I believe you told us that that was not the correct name?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Tushi. It should be Tushile.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, that was part of a supplement -- information that we provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Also on page 6 in the second paragraph, you mentioned that, when you went to assist with the burials of the victims that were killed on the 28th of March, that it was a Wednesday, the 1st of April 1999, but looking at the calendar we saw that Wednesday was on the 31st. Were you able to determine whether it was the 31st of March, on the Wednesday, or on the 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: It was a Wednesday, four days after the massacre. It was a Wednesday. That's the day that they were buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I recall from our discussions that you indicated the massacre occurred on Sunday, the 28th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Sunday, yes. It was the day of Bajram, the day of sacrifice. That's when the people were massacred.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in counting four days you included Sunday, the 28th?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's it. There are four days in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I just have a few questions about your statement and I have one photograph I want to show you and ask you about, and also a map. But first of all, in your statement, your first statement from 1999, in the last paragraph in the English on page 2, you mentioned that on the 26th of March you and your family left your village of Broja to go to Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you say, "I was fearful of what the Serbs would do." What were you fearful of and why?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Because there had been other massacres in Prekaz, Qires, and other places. And Likoshan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. So you travelled to Izbica and we understand from your statement you stayed there on the night of the 26th and the 27th. In your statement, you say that you could hear shooting and shelling going on constantly. Could you tell from where -- from where or from which direction the shelling and shooting was --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: It was from Pelicej [phoen], Junik, from that direction. We were in a valley, we were -- there were hills around us on all sides. We only heard them, we couldn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to take to you the morning of the 28th, which you told us was a Sunday in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On page 3 in the English, the second paragraph up from the bottom, you mention the first thing you saw around 9.30 that morning were three policemen setting fire to a haystack and then coming closer.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. It was hay, a haystack.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you describe how they came and asked for money?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What can you tell us about these three individuals? What ethnicity were they, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I don't know the nationality but I know that they were dressed in black. They were dark-skinned. I approached them and they asked money from me, a thousand marks from us, and I gave them 3 -- 30 marks. The others had 200, 300. People gave whatever they had, in order that they not harm the people and burn the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: And the tractors.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: These people, what language did they speak to you in?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: In Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand from your statement you understand and speak Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I believe I understand that's from your time in your compulsory military service that you learned the language?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the last paragraph on page 3 of the English, you describe that a few minutes later, more - what you described as police - approached. You said there were about 80 of them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I would think around 80. I can't tell you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the top of page 4, you mention that about 25 of these 80 individuals were wearing a blue camouflage uniform. What about the other 50 plus? What were they wearing? What did they look like?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: They were dressed like paramilitaries and there were normal soldiers there with some of them had black scarves around their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Whether you say they were dressed like paramilitaries, can you give the Court some more information about that or can you describe their uniforms or their appearance otherwise?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. May I speak?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The paramilitaries were like Seselj's Chetniks and they had a head-piece with a visor. I was sure that it was them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you describe other than their head-piece with a visor what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: They looked almost like the normal army uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Of what colour, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Like grass colour, like green.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was it one solid colour or some kind of design or pattern?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: It was a bit pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I still don't understand, though. Was it just one solid colour or did it have any kind of design or stripes, polka dots, checks?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Some of them had camouflage uniforms but I don't really know what to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: How many of them there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Of the 80, then, we had 25 wearing blue camouflage uniforms and some of the others which you've described as paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you indicate that there was a third group?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: There were paramilitary and then there were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did you -- did the ones you describe as normal soldiers wear?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: They were wearing Yugoslav military dress.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mention the some wearing black head scarves, I believe. Which ones were those?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. There were some with black head scarves. I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were they -- the ones with black head scarves, were they wearing the blue camouflage, the green camouflage, or the regular army uniform, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know. I just remember that they had black head scarves around their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's all right. Thank you. On page 4 of the English, in the third paragraph, you describe how this group of men then separated out the men from the rest of the thousands of people that were in the field that day, and you were in that group of about 150 men. Can you describe for us the --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- I'm sorry. And in your statement you describe the man who appeared to be in charge, giving orders. You said he had some sort of badge or insignia on the sleeve of each arm of his green olive-coloured camouflage uniform. Can you tell us anything else about that insignia or badge?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. That was what he was wearing. I don't know -- what else do you want me to say about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you -- did you -- can you tell us anything about the badge or the -- or the insignia on his sleeves?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: They had insignia like Yugoslav soldiers. And he was about 165 centimetres tall, a bit fat. He had green eyes, I think, and a crooked nose. He was about 27 to 30 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your statement, you tell us about what happened while you were sitting there and the abuse that you underwent before this man you described as the commander spoke in Serbian and told -- and told his men that, "Everyone knows their duty; now do it." When you and -- you were in a group of men that were marched off by one policeman, and I believe you said there were about 30 or 33 of you in your group; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Thaqi, you tell in your statement how you were marched some 200, 250 metres away, told to kneel down, and then the shooting started. Was there only one --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there only one policeman or one individual with a gun who took the 33 of you to the -- and what kind of machine-gun did he --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: There was only that one person who killed the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: He had a machine-gun, 100, and we found the cartridges later there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. When you say "a machine-gun, 100," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: It's a 100 machine-gun, it's called. Sorry, I can't really describe it any more. We just called 100 machine-gun and it had a belt with 50 cartridges and they shot -- they fired three times.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: He fired three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Three times, does that mean three single shots?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But there were 33 in your group and how many were killed?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: There were 30 who were killed and only three survived. I and two others, Sheqir, Qallapeki.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The statement says, "he sprayed the bullets up and down the lines three times."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm going to follow up on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- in the transcript, it said you -- by three times you meant three single shots. I'm trying to understand how 30 men were killed if he only fired three single shots. Did I misunderstand your earlier answer?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Well, there were three bursts of fire and about 150 shots, not three bullets. I had four -- I got four bullets in my clothing alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand now.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I would like to show you a photograph. I think you've seen it before. It's Exhibit P244, if we could bring that up on the screen for Mr. Thaqi to look at. This may take a moment, Mr. Thaqi, but I want to ask you if you can help us understand where some of the locations are that are shown on this photograph. And after --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... group had been shot and you were still alive, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: We stayed there for 40 minutes. There were two bodies on me. We lay there for 40 minutes. I shouted in pain and I heard other shouts but there was this other person who moved and he asked me, "Who are you?" I said, "I am Milazim," and he said, "I'm Sheqir." He said, "Don't move, please don't move. Stay calm. Let's get alive from here."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness slow down for the benefit of the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, the witnesses are asking to you slow down a bit so that they can keep up.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I -- Demush Asllani, he gave a cry and I gave a cry as well. And Sheqir touched my left leg and he asked me, "Who are you?" And I said, "I'm Milazim from Broja." I asked him his name and he said, "I'm Sheqir from Drenikej [phoen]." Vojinike. So later we got up and went to the mountains, in the direction of the mountains, of the forest, and there was a tractor track there in the mountain. The Serbs were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment. While I'm still waiting for the photo to come up on my monitor, and let me ask you another question. While -- while you were lying there with the other survivors in your group as well as the dead men in your group, could you hear anything going on around you?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: You mean when we buried the bodies, the people who died?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. While you were still lying underneath the men who had been shot in your group, before you got up with the other survivors and went away, did you hear anything going on?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: We heard some cracks, cracking noises. The other group, 20 metres away, I heard the shots. That's what I heard, three groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you now, do you have a photograph on the screen in front of you? Do you --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... recognise that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What's that a picture of?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The first group was here in the photograph while we were here on top of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I think we can mark on this photograph with the pen he's handing you. Can you see --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... letter A that's already on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us where the letter A, the line is pointing to that comes from the letter of A? What's that location?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: It's Izbica. We were right above the cemetery. There was a ditch there, a canal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your statement before I think you've described A as referring to the location where the first group was shot; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on this photograph, the letter B or almost looks like the number 13, can you tell us what location that is referring to? Who or what was in that location?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: This was the second group in the field at a pear tree. I found there 24 sticks that old people used to walk, and shoes, while the third group is 20 metres above this, in our direction, and nobody survived from that group. One escaped but he was killed later by the Serbs, before he got to that tractor track. They called on him, "Stop." He didn't stop and they killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: While the fourth group was on the right side about 500 metres away, it was at the foot of the mountain; Mustafa Draga was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And let me ask you if on this photograph you can use the pen to write the number 2 and draw a circle around what you described in your second statement as the second group of, I think, 27 men?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: This is the first one, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you could --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The second one was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you write the number 2 and draw a circle around where the second group was?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The second group is here, at the pear tree, and the third one here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we take a screen shot of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do, we've now got how many marks on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You didn't give him time to finish, Mr. Hannis. There are four groups --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and one of the things I'm rather confused about is the A and B are written but they are directed to other points which are at the end of lines which run from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, before we mark that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is becoming a rather confusing exercise if it really is vital at all, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask a couple of questions and see if I can clarify, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, the letter A where you've drawn a triangle, to the left of it where you've drawn the mark, is that where you were? Is that where the shooting occurred? Or is it at the other end of the line from the letter A?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. No, no. This is the first group. We were at the mountain, the first group. The second group was in the field. The third one was above us, 20 metres away from us, and the fourth one on this other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. The question I'm trying to ask, Mr. Thaqi, is where were you actually standing or kneeling at the time you were shot? Are you by the letter A in this photograph or are you farther up above where the line from the letter A is pointing toward what appears to be a ditch?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry I asked the question.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: We -- yes. I was lying there and I had two bodies on -- above me, you know, and as I said I was lying there for 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I feel like we are miscommunicating. Where were you? Are you next to the letter A or are you farther north on this photograph, if the top is north? I understand that you were marched off to the woods --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: In that direction. We went in -- in that direction with Sheqir and we followed that tractor track towards Belica and we stopped there. We rested for a little bit, and I saw some Marlboro cigarette packets, and the boots that they had left there, the night of the Saturday, I mean. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a second. From your statement I understood you were marched about 200 or 250 metres, you came alongside a water channel or a canal, I guess, used to water fields in the summer. That's where you were ordered to stop and kneel down and that's where you were shot. Does this photograph show where that water canal is?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you draw a line tracing that water canal on the photograph for me, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The water canal was here, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was it next to the water canal that your group was when you were shot?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. That's where we were shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have any more questions about that at the moment. I think I'll forgo the screen shot, however. I think the verbal description with what is in his written statement and the photograph are probably more helpful than this particular photograph, and I don't want to start over.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Thaqi, you describe in your statement then what happened after you and the survivors went off, and how you stayed in Vojinik for a couple of days and then how on the 31st of March you went to assist with the burial of the victims.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see anyone filming those activities that day?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: He was Dr. Lili Lloshi [phoen], with my cousin Sefa [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during that process of burying the men who were killed on the 28th, did you assist in identifying who some of those people were? Or providing the names?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. The people that I knew, there were people from Izbica. We wrote the names, and we put a stick, a piece -- a board on each grave and we wrote the name and surname of each person. The name and surname was also written on a notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Since that day, have you seen the film or the video that Dr. Lloshi made of the burial of the victims?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Once only.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you about something that -- that you told us about when we met yesterday. After you -- you say in your statement you returned home on the 14th of June 1999, and a couple of days after that --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: On the 14th? Did you say the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: June the 14th. June the 14th, after the fighting ended, you returned?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have occasion shortly after that to return to Izbica, to the burial site?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.
