utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My objection is based on a supplemental information sheet which we received yesterday evening from the Prosecutor. I believe he's about to embark on a line of questioning which the Prosecution informs us did not form a part of its 65 ter summary. And in our submission, it's not permissible short of showing good cause and due diligence for the Prosecution to proceed in this line of questioning given that the witness was interviewed over a two-day period in 1999, a two-day period in 2001, he testified in the Milosevic trial, and the pre-trial brief does not include this evidence in its summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can only indicate to the Court that in speaking with this witness yesterday, we asked some additional questions that apparently no one had asked him before. He gave us some information about the burial site, which we would like to present to the Court. We notified Defence counsel of this in the supplemental information sheet. We indicated that these two new sentences or paragraphs were not part of the 65 ter summary, and that in furnishing this information we intended to lead information about it and wanted this to serve as notice of that fact. I don't know if the Court received a copy of our supplemental information sheet or not. No. I understand you have not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't have supplemental information. But we had the same issue with a witness - was it yesterday? - and decided that when this situation arises, you should seek leave of the court and justify leading evidence which is on issues not heralded in the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I understood the Court to say that that could be done in writing or orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It could, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I guess as a matter of timing, perhaps I should have raised it the first moment we started today. I understood also the Court's -- one of the Court's primary concerns was that the Defence receive notice at the earliest possible occasion and to bring it to their attention that this is something that was not in the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In general terms, what does this relate to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It relates to -- well, Your Honour, I don't know if I should speak to this in front of the witness or not. Perhaps we could have him take his headphones off. I don't know if he speaks and understands English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think if -- Mr. O'Sullivan, do you think that this discussion requires to be out with the hearing of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The practical solution may be the one proposed by Mr. Hannis. If the witness doesn't understand English we can do it in his presence; otherwise we are doing it in his presence and probably shouldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, we have a matter of law to resolve here. While we do that, it is necessary for you briefly to leave the courtroom. The usher will take you outside and we'll summon you back as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. So please leave the courtroom briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The two paragraphs in supplemental information, one is that the witness says that on the -- that he was told by others that on the 28th of May 1999, the bodies that had been buried in Izbica were exhumed by the Serbs who spent, I think, three days or used excavators to remove those bodies. Then the other thing was, shortly after returning to his home in June 1999, a BBC television team asked him to show them where the bodies were buried. The witness accompanied the team to the burial site and they found the area had been ploughed or leveled as if there were no graves or people buried there, that the planks, some of the planks used to mark the graves were thrown all over the place. They also saw some body parts left behind after this apparent excavation. We anticipate you will hear other evidence in this case about that excavation and where some of the bodies ended up. An autopsy of 100 and some -- 101 were performed by a witness listed in this case, who will be called to testify about that. So it's corroborative of other testimony you will hear in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you remind me of the issue that arose in relation to the other witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that Ms. Moeller's witness, Ms. Bala?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe it --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was. It was Ms. Bala and with respect to the methodology used by the OSCE [indiscernible] disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, when she -- when she worked for OSCE, in -- the manner of recording interviews, et cetera, and as I understood at the time, part of the argument was that that was something that was not mentioned in the 65 ter as evidence that she would discuss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we consider the situation to be different here from the situation in the previous case that we dealt with on the 22nd of August. There is one difference that rather modifies the significance of this, and that is that the witness is dealing or would be dealing in these additional areas with an expansion of an issue that's already identified as an issue in the 65 ter summary, and that is the alleged massacre that we are dealing with. It's simply an expansion of his knowledge of events relating to that. And the other difference here, the one that really matters is that in our opinion, Mr. Hannis has shown good cause why this additional material ought to be admitted, and he's done so by indicating that his investigations were more searching than those made before and elicited this additional information. So in the circumstances, we will grant the application to lead this additional evidence but we will take account of any request that is made by the Defence for essential -- any essential remedy that they require, such as -- as a result of this, such as recalling the witness, but we do feel that if this does give rise to the need for further inquiry, that perhaps it's an inquiry which that can be made quite quickly, and then that recall might not require the return from Kosovo of the witness but might simply require a delay in his departure. So now let's have the witness back and we'll continue with his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, we've dealt with that matter of law, and your evidence will now continue. Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi in June, shortly after the 14th of June 1999, when you had returned home, did you have occasion to visit the burial site in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How did that come about? Why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was working at home. I didn't really have any where to sleep. And I had a visitor and he gave me his visiting card and we went together there. And I went with him, and we saw whether they were actually there, the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Who was the visitor?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Someone from the BBC. He gave me his visiting card. I have it at home still. He was a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what happened when you and he went to the burial site?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were four of them all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Four people from BBC, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What happened then when the five of you went to the burial site?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we went there, we had a look and they saw that the bodies had been exhumed with a digger, and taken somewhere else. Some of them had been excavated by hand. We could see some of the bones of the legs and the hands. And this is all true. And we wrote down the -- and the stakes where their names were written on were all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, you had been present on the 31st of March 1999, when the victims had been buried. Do you recall how many people were buried on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was that number, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, did you -- did you hear from anyone or did you get any information about what had happened between the 31st of March 1999, when those 147 were buried and the 14th -- sometime shortly after the 14th of June, when you discovered what you discovered?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did you hear and who did you hear it from?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What who heard? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, the transcript said there was no answer from my earlier question. Let me ask it again. Between the 31st of March, 1999, when you were aware of those 140 plus buried and the -- shortly after the 14th of June when you went out and saw the condition of the site, did anyone -- did you get any information from anyone about how that change occurred and where the bodies had gone? Yes or no, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The bodies were taken to Mitrovica and to Vushtrri and to Batajnica and Belgrade. 70 bodies were left over. I don't know what happened to the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who told you about what had happened to the bodies?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We buried them ourselves, almost all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. I understand that. But who told you that the bodies had been taken away?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who told me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were -- there were -- someone there and there were shelling that day, lots of shelling, and the people fled, and one of those people saw what was going on from the mountain side. I didn't see it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you speak personally with this person?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did he tell you about who removed the bodies?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who removed the bodies?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the police and the army, the Yugoslav police and army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I have a moment, Your Honour? Thank you, I have no other questions of the witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll proceed in this order: General Pavkovic, General Lazarevic, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, General Ojdanic and General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Thaqi. I am Aleksandar Aleksic. I am attorney-at-law and, together with Mr. John Ackerman, I represent General Nebojsa Pavkovic. I will be putting some questions to you, I will try to be as specific as possible when putting my questions, and I ask that your answers be as brief as possible, preferably a yes or a no. When preparing for this cross-examination, we had a certain line of questions that I will try to adhere to but in view of what you said here today in your evidence-in-chief, there are some modifications that I will have to make to my prepared questions. Mr. Thaqi, you gave several statements. The first one was in late 1999 and then there was an additional statement in 2001, if I'm not mistaken. Then you testified in the case against Mr. Milosevic, and then you provided some additional information, if I understood it well, yesterday. You gave these additional details to the OTP. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I read once again very carefully your first statement, and the transcript from the Milosevic case, when you were cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic, although I read it in B/C/S, I have to admit. But it seems that it is only today, after all this time, that on page 41, line 5, of the transcript, you said that there were regular soldiers there in VJ uniforms, and then when asked by Mr. Hannis on the following page, you described this person, how tall he was, what eyes and what nose he had, and then, in line 5, you said that this person had an insignia resembling those by the Yugoslav soldiers. Are both of these things correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me, then, that during the past seven years you never mentioned these facts, you never provided this information to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did. I said it in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. Do I need to put each of these portions to the witness individually? Or, rather, let's take the description of this person that Mr. Hannis insisted upon. I think it was on page 4 of both B/C/S and English versions, paragraph 3. It says there, or rather the witness describes that person and says, "I would describe him as a person of 27 years of age, a medium build, about 165 centimetres tall, dark brown hair that had a reddish nuance to it. His face was narrow and long and his nose was large and crooked. He had a green camouflage uniform and a cap of the same colour. I think that he had some kind of an emblem or an insignia on his sleeve near the shoulder." This is the description that he gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: My question is, can you once again describe to us this insignia or emblem concerning which today you said that it resembled the ones worn by Yugoslav soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just have to repeat myself. That's what it was like. It's right what I said. I recognised it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, I'm just asking you this: During the past seven years, you never said that this was an emblem resembling the one worn by Yugoslav soldiers. Initially you said that there was just an emblem or insignia. You didn't qualify it. Can you tell us what shape it was, what colour? I don't want to put any leading questions to you but could you help us with this, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The clothing was of Yugoslav army colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Thaqi. Now I have to read several lines preceding that. Before this description, you said that one of the policemen seemed as though he was in charge and so on and then the description follows. Can you tell us this once again, please, then?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was him. That's the one I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, I'm trying to be as specific as possible. Some time ago you said that this person had an emblem of the Yugoslav army and then now I just read out to you what it says in your statement, where you describe him as a policeman. Do you see a difference there or is it all the same to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they are not the same. Soldiers are one thing and policemen are a different thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, I fully agree with you that soldiers are one and policemen are quite different but you describe the same person both as a policeman and as a soldier. That is the gist of my question. You said he was a policeman but he wore an emblem of the Yugoslav army. Did he also have a red bandana, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't. He was wearing Yugoslav colours. I didn't see a bandana on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm doing my best but I have to insist on this, if you think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Thaqi said that this man had an emblem worn by those by the Yugoslav soldiers. Three lines before that he described him as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thus my question is: Can you tell us, was he a policeman or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He wasn't a policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've got the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, but, Mr. Thaqi, you said that this policeman was doing certain things and then in the following several paragraphs you continue using the word policeman when speaking of that same person. Mr. Thaqi, for the first time after more than seven years, you used the term Yugoslav army and normal soldiers. Perhaps I wasn't clear enough but in your statement you said this is what this policeman looked like, and then you said he had this emblem, and then you continue referring to this person as a policeman, and now in your evidence here, you are telling us that this person was not a policeman. Can you please describe this discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say that he was not a policeman. Say whatever you want but he wasn't a policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you say that he actually was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what he was. He spoke Serbian. He must have been a soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I see it's time for our break so we will break now and resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd just like to confirm, I think I have the sense from the Defence that cross-examination is going to take us to the end of the session and I would like to let the next witness go back to the hotel. I think that's safe. Do I see any disagreement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that likely to be the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am going to finish. I don't know about the rest of my colleagues. They will probably have some questions too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're call, Mr. Hannis, on this one. I have no idea at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think I'm going to take the risk and let him go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Aleksic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Fila. The interpreters have trouble hearing Mr. Fila. Could he please speak into the microphone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The interpreter can't hear what you're saying, Mr. Fila. You're not speaking closely enough to -- that's it. The microphone at that height is better.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you allowed today -- well, I'm not questioning the fact that you allowed it. You allowed it because you allowed it. But it led to further discussions on our side so we will probably require more time. Do we understand each other now? I mean what Mr. Hannis found out yesterday, last night, and this additional questioning of the witness actually changed our plans so we most certainly will not be able to finish by 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, the position is clear, then, Mr. Hannis. So carry on now, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, you testified in the Milosevic case on the 14th of June 2002, and that is page 7146, the last few minutes. I'm going to read all of this out to you and then please tell me whether it is correct. Mr. Milosevic says: "You survived this execution. That is the substance of your statement. And you say that this group was taken off by one policeman that you were taken off by one policeman, right?" And your answer was: "Yes." After that, Mr. Milosevic asked you the following: "And apart from this one policeman, there was nobody else with you, just this one policeman, right?" And you said: "I didn't see any other policemen. Only that one. The others remained below in the meadow. Is that right?" That is on page 7147, in continuation.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said -- I called him a policeman but he was a paramilitary and he was with our group. I don't know about the other groups, what happened to them, the groups which were executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Thaqi, you are claiming now that this man is a member of paramilitary forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to move on to another topic. That was actually supposed to be the beginning of our line of cross-examination. Mr. Thaqi, in your statement at the very beginning, that is to say -- sorry, I just need a moment. On page 2 of the B/C/S and English versions, it is the one but last or rather the third paragraph from the bottom. You say, "I heard that the police killed three people as they were shelling." Of course, you don't have any personal knowledge of this whether this was true or not, right? You just heard about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean that you're not an eyewitness, that you don't have any direct knowledge. You heard about that so you cannot know whether that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who are you talking about, because I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why do you ask -- why do you ask a question like this when the statement is clear, that he heard about it from someone else? Why do you need to ask this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I shall move on to my next topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In your statement, on page 3 of the Serbian version or rather, sorry, the English version. So in English it is page 3, paragraph 5. In B/C/S it's 1, 2, 3, 4. 4, paragraph 4. You say, "Again that night I could hear the sound of constant shelling and shooting coming, I assumed, from the surrounding villages being attacked by the Serbs." You say, "I assumed."

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We just heard it. We were out in the field --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on, please. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. That, "I assumed from the surrounding villages being attacked by the Serbs." So I wanted to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but what is the question you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, was it perhaps the case that these sounds that the witness heard, were they maybe coming from fighting between the KLA and the Serb forces? That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you want to do that, then you ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, perhaps the sounds that you heard were the result of fighting between the KLA and the Serb forces, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not the way it was because there was no KLA. The KLA did not have military vehicles for launching shell -- rockets or shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to go back to the Milosevic transcript. The page is 7146, and you say -- towards the end of the page, you say that at that meadow, you assume there were between 15.000 and 16.000 people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Out of these 15.000 or 16.000, only 157 were men, right? That's what you said in the Milosevic case on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. The rest were women and children.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all old people, women and children and old men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And the rest? I mean, what about working-age men, if we can put it that way? Where were they? Fighting for the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. They were -- the old men were in the meadow. There were disabled people there. What could they have fought with? They didn't have any arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Thaqi. Perhaps you did not follow this properly. Maybe I didn't put the question properly. I was not referring to old men who were present. You say that out of 16.000 people, there were only 157 military-aged men, able-bodied men, if I can put it that way, but there were more inhabitants. Where were these military-aged men, able-bodied men? I was asking about them. Were they fighting on the side of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Thaqi, you're from the village of Brocna, right? If I understood you correctly today?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Do you know that the special brigade of the KLA had its headquarters in your village?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't know, no, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, just a few more questions. You said that on the 1st of April or rather, later you said on the 31st of March, you returned to Izbica and that there you saw 150 to 200 persons, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: 150 to 200. What exactly do you mean by them? You mean when we were burying the bodies?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes. As I said, on the 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were probably even more, and KLA, they were burying, we were burying together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I wanted to ask you, Mr. Thaqi. How many members of the KLA were present?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. How could I know how many there were? I didn't know them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that you knew the 150 or 200 people, all of them, personally. I mean, I'm just asking. Well, thank you. I would just like to put one more question or perhaps two more questions. You say that in your statement on page 6, that you were again with your family on the 7th of April in Tushile and that your family said that the rest were moving towards Albania but that the Serbs returned them and that they returned to their homes. Is that right? The Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, where the massacre took place in Izbica, all the other people who were there, the families, women and - not the old people - were expelled in the direction of Albania because they were trying to carry out ethnic cleansing of the whole area up to Gjakova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, that was not my question. My question was as follows: On your statement -- in your statement on page 6 of the B/C/S version, that is to say in English it is page 6, paragraph 4, you said my family and I were reunited at Tushile on or about the 7th of April. I learned from them that they and the others had spent six days walking towards Albania only to be turned back by the Serbs. Did you say that? That's all I'm asking. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: 15 days they were walking with their children, all the way there and all the way back, to Tushile.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: But they returned, they didn't go to Albania. That's my question, or rather that's the point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is completely --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is completely unnecessary questioning. The statement is as clear as day and doesn't need this confusion cast upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic. Mr. Bakrac? Or Mr. Cepic? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today you mentioned on transcript page 39, the last lines, or rather line 25, and on page 40, line 1, and at page 41 you described this group of persons who came on the 28th of March 1999 and you said that they were wearing different uniforms, blue, green, camouflage, that some of them had black bandanas around their heads; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Beards, mustaches; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There may have been but I didn't see any with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Longish hair, some of them?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they had long hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You could not see very clearly the insignia they had, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't able to look at them, get a good look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Actually, you're not quite certain what unit that was and who that unit belonged to, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They were police, paramilitaries, militaries and they had bandanas on their heads. They were there. I don't know the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that your best recollection of these events was in 1999, right? When you made this statement. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? I saw the events with my own eyes. That's what I said in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you about 1999, November 1999. That's when you made your statement. You will agree with me that that is when you remembered best; isn't that right? Much better than you can recall today, seven years later?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I was more clear about -- and I was younger.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you made statements earlier, that is to say in 1999, in 2001, in the proceedings against Slobodan Milosevic on the 14th of June 2002 and also in yesterday's addendum, you did not mention the army or anyone else except for what you had stated as stated; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I said before is the same as what I'm saying now. It's the same story.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did someone perhaps suggest to you what you should say today in this courtroom before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think these things happen here. Maybe in Serbia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I haven't got any further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will have some questions, only because of the addendum. Otherwise I had not intended to ask any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, My name is Toma Fila and, together with my colleague, Mr. Petrovic, I am Defence counsel for Nikola Sainovic. I would ask you kindly to concentrate only on the BBC and what happened afterwards. I'm not going to ask you any of what happened before that. So you said to us that at one point in time when you returned, journalists came and you went to this place where you participated in the burial of the dead and you realised that the corpses were not there. My first question would be, were you surprised due to the fact that the corpses were not there? In other words, up until that moment, did you not know that the corpses had been removed?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, when was it that you first found out, when, at what point in time, did you realise that they had been removed? Exhumed, sorry; not removed, exhumed. I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact date but it was two days after we returned home. There were these people from the BBC. But before them, there were 18 people that came. I don't know whether they were journalists or what they were, and they saw the place that had been bulldozed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, that's not an answer to my question. When was it that you personally, Mr. Thaqi, you personally, when did you first find out that something had happened there? Because you said a few moments ago that you did not know until you came to the actual spot that the corpses had been exhumed from the places where you had buried them. You personally.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally went there with the people from the BBC the second day after I returned home, and that's when I saw what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If I understood this correctly, you saw that the corpses were not there where you had helped bury them. When was it that you first found out that somebody had exhumed them? Can you please help me with this because I'm asking this question for the third time and it's the same question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When did he personally learn of this? Perhaps we are not understanding each other right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He has said to you, Mr. Fila, that it was when he went to the burial ground with the BBC journalists, and he says that was two days --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And he says that was when he first found out.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's when he learned that the corpses were not there. He saw that they were not there. But when did they tell him that the Serbs or whoever had exhumed the bodies and when were they taken wherever? If I followed his statement properly he said that he saw with the BBC journalists for the first time that the corpses were not there. Now, who told him, and when, that the bodies had been exhumed? That's what I'm trying to get at. I mean, if you cannot understand what I'm saying then he's going to have even greater difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, you told us that someone told you that the bodies had been removed by the police and the army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just listen to me for a moment. The person who told you that, did that person tell you about it before you visited the site with the BBC or after you had visited the site with the BBC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After, it was after, or maybe it was three weeks or a month later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Fila, that answers the question because it means that the first time he was aware of this was when he visited the site, which is what I understood he was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the BBC. That's when he realised that the people who had been buried were not there. But three weeks later he found out why they were not there, if I understood it correctly this time. I hope that we all agree on that. Now, who said this to him? How they had been exhumed? Who came? When? I mean, okay. I'll ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me ask you. I'm sorry, I put questions my own way so then I put questions through the Court, through the Judges. Sorry about that. I forgot for a moment that that's not the way you put questions here. All right. I'm asking you now. As far as I understand things, you don't know that man's name or perhaps you forgot it. But all right. Never mind. What was it that he said to you exactly? Who came when?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This person -- I told you that he told me three weeks later that they were on the mountain and they had seen with their own eyes -- he's an elderly man, he's 72 or 73 years old, and he told me that the bodies were exhumed and this happened on the 28th to the 31st of March, for four days. This is all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Further on you said in response to a question put by my learned friend Mr. Hannis that these corpses were taken to Sremska Mitrovic, Batajnica, and some third location that you referred to. How come you know about -- oh, was it Kosovska Mitrovica? All right, Kosovska Mitrovica, Batajnica, and I don't know the third place. How come you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the KFOR are bringing the bodies from Batajnica, from Mitrovica, from Vushtrri, from all these places, these people that I had helped bury. This is a sure thing. I'm not lying here. And I swore here that I would tell the truth. I have got children, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that's something -- Mr. Fila, that's something that would need to be proved by some other means, by the Prosecution in this case. And that was fairly plain from the answer he gave about the bodies being taken to these four places. That sort of thing will require other evidence here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. That's right. I was just trying to learn how he had learned that the bodies had been returned. I just learned it, and this is the end of my questioning. It was important to find out that it was the KFOR who did it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: About what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wanted to say why they took the corpses and sent them to Belgrade and because of that 147 families are suffering to this day. I don't know why they did that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give me a moment until I check something. Mr. Hannis, the actual shooting here is alleged to be on the specific day, is it the 28th?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sepenuk?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do have a few questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Thaqi. I hope I will be putting a limited number of questions to you, and I would ask you to give us brief answers, as you have been doing so far, so that we can finish before we adjourn today. Did you mention that during the exhumation of these corpses, there was a shelling?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I was told. There was a lot of shelling, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was shelling that area?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know who: The Yugoslav army, because we did not have any such weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what remained unclear to me. If it was the Serbian authorities who were conducting the exhumation, is it your evidence that those same forces also shelled the location where the exhumation was taking place?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The Serbs shelled first, and then exhumed the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they shell the area where the bodies were or did they shell the surrounding area, the forest?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All around, not -- not there where the bodies were, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that it's much clearer now.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you something about the period of time when you left your village of Broja. Did Saban Draga come to your village? He was a KLA officer who ordered that all able-bodied men be removed from the village, or leave the village.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see Saban Draga. I have not seen him even later. I did not see him. I have heard about him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anyone else from the KLA come to your village and order the population to move to Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We left ourselves because they were shelling. That's what they used to do. They shelled first and the population left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have the relevant document here, how we received a chart from the OTP. It's ERN number is 00763607 to 00763595. This is a statement given by Refki Thaqi, born on the 2nd of May 1961. In his statement he describes the departure from the village of Broja. I will be reading the statement in English to make sure that you receive an accurate translation. "The witness, his brother Thaqi, Lufti, and his uncle Thaqi, Dzafer, went to a hill above Izbica called Kodra e Elezit to observe Serb forces coming from different directions and saw KLA fighting the Serb forces. On 24 March, 1999, Draga Saban, KLA officer, informed the people that the young men should leave Izbica for Tushile." Do you know Mr. Refki Thaqi?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him very well. He was not there present at the Izbica incident. He is young. He is now about 33 or 34 years old. I don't know who he gave the statement to because I don't think it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thaqi. There is another document contained in this chart. It comes from the ICG database, which was discussed here at length. It's marked A/0717. We don't know who provided this statement, but in it, it says as follows: "About 30.000 [Realtime transcript read in error, "3.000"] persons were in that place during heavy fighting went on between KLA and Serb forces."

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's how I understand this document. [Interpretation] Yes, that's how I understand this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not true at all. I don't think this is correct at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, who was the number of persons you read out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought so. The transcript reflects 3.000. It should be 30.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. And this statement -- this document has a date, 28th of March 1999 and the description says, Izbica in the municipality of Srbica and the village of Azrim [phoen]. So obviously, people who were displaced from Azrim to Izbica, not particularly from Broja. But anyways, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you spoke about the reason for leaving your home in 1998 - I apologise, 1999 - you said that it was due to the fact that there were massacres in Qires, Prekaz, and Likoshane and that that happened in early May 1998. Also in Recak [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th in Recak, people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But when giving explanation you said that you were prompted to do that by the conflict in Prekaz, Likoshane, and Qires. That's all you said.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I will tell you how it was. And that is true. On the 15th of January 1998 -- now I forget, I'm sorry. I -- it was on the 28th in Qires, and Likoshan, on the 5th in Prekaz and Broja and we were attacked immediately and this is all true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The dates you've given for events in Qires, Likoshan, Prekaz, and Broja, which month are you talking of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The month was January, January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A walker [as interpreted] was in 1998. 15th of January. 28th. As I said, in Qires and Likoshan on a Saturday and a Sunday but this was on -- this was in February 1998. Then 5th of March in Prekaz and Broja. And we left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Thaqi, in your statement given on the 9th of November 1999, English version page 3, paragraph 7, Albanian version page 4, paragraph 3, B/C/S version, page 3, paragraph 8, or rather paragraph 6, you describe the people who asked money from you, up to 1.000 German marks, in order to ensure that your homes and tractors were safe. Then you describe them as people wearing green/olive camouflage uniforms and that across their chests and shoulders they had ammunition belts. And then you pointed to a uniform when being questioned by investigator Stewart; however, we didn't see that in the courtroom. Thus I'd like to ask you whether this description, is that of paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're confusing me. Well, I think I explained this once already.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this description refers to the paramilitaries as well, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything about the strength of the KLA in Drenica region?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many there were, and I did not pay attention to those issues. However, I can say that I would want them to be as many as possible, and have tanks and the weapons that you had because they were fighting an unequal enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Even though you do not know about the strength of the KLA units. Tell us, do you know whether these forces were normally deployed either in villages or in the immediate vicinity of villages?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They moved around everywhere, in the whole of Kosova but they did not have heavy weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Bear with me one moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Thaqi. I have no further questions for you?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, with regard to the policeman or the paramilitary who took you and the other 32 men off before shooting you, do you recall what kind of uniform he was wearing? What colour?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was wearing a grass colour, greenish, it was a paramilitary. That's what I said at the time and that's what I say now, it was a paramilitary. He was about 40, 42 years old, a bit fat and short, stubby.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was his uniform the same as or different from the uniform that the man you described as the commander was wearing?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think it was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Fila asked you a question about the exhumation of the bodies. On page 73 of the transcript, at lines 6 to 7, I believe it says you were told between the 28th and 31st of March is when the bodies why exhumed. Now, we know that can't be correct because you told us that the bodies were buried on the 31st of March. Can you help us with that? What date were you told that the bodies had been exhumed? Sometime between the 31st of March and the 14th or 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that on the 28th of May - not March, May - and it was a -- four days, it was a Sunday, Monday, Tuesday. I was quite surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You noticed me too late. This is an example of impermissible leading question. I asked the witness, he gave me his answer, and now the Prosecutor is putting leading questions to him so that he would give a time frame that suits the Prosecution. That's all I had to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what do you say was the leading question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When he said, first the Prosecutor said that it couldn't have been between the 28th and 31st March because this is when they were buried, and that was fine. And then he said it would have to be between this and that date, and that wasn't all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question should have been: "When was it?" That should have been the question both in civil law system and in common law system. That's how the question should be phrased. He perhaps could have said that I accept that it couldn't have been on the 28th if they were buried on the 31st.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't March, it was May, the 28th of May, four days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have that. Mr. Fila, the parameters that were given to the witness were between the 31st of March and the 14th or 15th of June; now, in our opinion, that is not leading. That's stating the obvious, and the witness's answer, we will have to evaluate whether it was spontaneous or whether it was in any way prompted by the question. That's a matter we'll take particular account of when we come to assess the evidence. Thank you. Mr. Hannis, do you have any other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi in some of your documents your name is spelled in English T-h-a-c-i and in some places T-h-a-q-i. Can you help us with which one it should be?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thaqi with a Q.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Well, Mr. Thaqi, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming again to the Tribunal to give it. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much that you are taking care of justice so that such events will not be repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in fact, if you just sit there for a moment while we adjourn the Court then the usher will show you out in a moment or two. We'll now adjourn until -- sorry, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I mention to the Defence counsel one matter concerning scheduling? Because we are at the end of the week, we have three witnesses remaining. Mustafa Draga will be the next witness tomorrow morning. Because of schedules we may -- we are considering reversing the order of the next two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we will advise them by e-mail tonight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please grab them before they leave and tell them the position, Mr. Hannis. I suppose it's just possible that we can be slightly more flexible tomorrow. We are sitting in the morning. So we will be adjourning until 9.00 army. Mr. Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, for holding you longer but we kindly ask the Prosecutor not to change the order of the witnesses because tomorrow we start in the morning and the whole this week we had the change in the schedule so it's very hard for us to follow because we have very limited resources. In every team we have two people, so we exchange and Mr. Ivetic had three witnesses in a row and now I have three witnesses in a row. So it's very hard for us. So we would kindly ask the Prosecutor to stick with the order he gave us before. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's also hard for to us stick it to the order when estimates about how long cross exam will be vary wildly from what actually happens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Since I suspect it's going to lighten our evening, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say something. You've got a lot of people here from Serbia, but you should bring a lot more, all those criminals who committed those crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not something for us to determine or for you to say here, Mr. Thaqi. The platter is in the hands of the Prosecution who direct the proceedings and any comment you wish to make about that should be directed to the Office of the Prosecutor. Mr. Hannis, you've told us who the next witness would be, that's Mustafa Draga. What is the change that you're proposing?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We propose to move Fedrije Xhafa to after the other name that I have even more difficult time pronouncing, the witness Gerxhaliu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it becomes 5, 7, and 6 in the order; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, I'm willing to keep the order the same but the difficulty I have is in proofing the witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that's not a problem for Mr. Lukic because he's up for these three witnesses, I gather.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, we would prefer to have Vucitrn in the next week because we have to do the complete analysis for Vucitrn municipality and we already calculated that it should fall in the next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
